title: Amul Goes Beyond Butter: India's Dairy Giant Enters the Organic Tea and Spices Arena
excerpt: With record revenues of ₹66,000 crore and a target of ₹1 lakh crore by FY26, Amul is betting that the trust built over decades of dairy can carry it into every corner of the Indian kitchen — and beyond.
body:
For generations of Indians, Amul has been more than a brand — it has been a household presence as constant as the morning newspaper. The Amul butter girl, perched on her blue-and-red billboard, has commented on everything from cricket matches to elections. Amul's milk, butter, and cheese have been staples in Indian kitchens since 1946.

Now, the Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation (GCMMF), which markets the Amul brand, is making its most ambitious move yet: a full-scale entry into certified organic tea, sugar, and spices.

## From Dairy to FMCG Powerhouse

Jayen Mehta, Managing Director of GCMMF, confirmed the expansion in a recent interview with CNBC-TV18, calling it a "natural progression" in Amul's evolution. The numbers back up the confidence. Amul closed FY25 with a record revenue of ₹66,000 crore and is targeting the landmark figure of ₹1 lakh crore by FY26.

"We are now officially the largest FMCG company in India, with a 10% higher turnover than our nearest multinational competitor," Mehta stated — a pointed reference to the likes of Hindustan Unilever that have long dominated India's consumer goods landscape.

The move into organic staples is strategic. India's organic food market is projected to exceed $10 billion by 2027, driven by rising health consciousness among urban consumers and the growing export demand for certified organic Indian products. By entering this space with the Amul brand, GCMMF is leveraging decades of consumer trust — the same trust that made "Amul Doodh Peeta Hai India" one of the most recognisable advertising campaigns in Indian history.

## What It Means for NRIs

For the Indian diaspora, Amul occupies an outsized place in cultural memory. It is the butter that went on every paratha, the cheese that topped every grilled sandwich, the ice cream that marked celebrations. Finding Amul products at Indian grocery stores abroad is a small act of homecoming.

The expansion into organic tea and spices has direct implications for NRI consumers. Indian grocery stores in the US, UK, and Canada already stock Amul dairy products. Organic chai, haldi, and jeera with the Amul stamp could soon join them on the shelf — offering diaspora families a trusted alternative to the organic brands they encounter at Whole Foods or Trader Joe's at significantly lower price points.

"Consumers trust Amul for quality, and we aim to extend that trust into new product categories where quality and authenticity matter most," Mehta noted. For NRIs navigating the organic food landscape abroad, where provenance and authenticity are often unclear, that trust carries weight.

## The Bigger Picture: Ice Cream, Protein, and a Global Footprint

Amul is not stopping at pantry staples. The company projects a 35-40% increase in ice cream sales this fiscal year and is investing heavily in protein beverages, with a fivefold increase in production capacity effective May 2026. These moves position Amul to compete not just with Indian FMCG players, but with global nutrition and wellness brands.

The cooperative model that made Amul — where 3.6 million dairy farmer members across Gujarat feed into one of the world's largest food processing networks — is now being tested at a different scale. Can a dairy cooperative successfully sell organic Darjeeling tea and single-origin turmeric powder? The brand recognition suggests yes. The execution will determine whether Amul becomes a truly multi-category global brand or remains defined by its dairy roots.

## What's Next

Amul's organic range is expected to roll out across India in phases, with international distribution to follow. For the diaspora, the key question is availability — whether Amul can replicate its dairy supply chain efficiency in organic staples and deliver products to NRI markets at competitive prices.

If it succeeds, the Amul girl may soon have a new billboard to comment on: the day Indian organic chai showed up next to matcha at your local American grocery store.

*Sources: Indian Food Times, CNBC-TV18 interview with Jayen Mehta, Future Market Insights Organic Food Market Report, GCMMF corporate announcements*
